analysis.one_liner: Makes insulin and its supplies free for Medicare beneficiaries during the COVID-19 emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill to eliminate Medicare cost-sharing for insulin during the COVID-19 emergency was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended Medicare Part D so that people with Medicare who use insulin would pay no deductible, copay, or coinsurance for insulin and the supplies needed to inject it for the duration of the declared COVID-19 public health emergency. It would also have let beneficiaries choose to receive their insulin and supplies by mail order during that period. The bill was introduced in late May 2020, sent to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 7 million Medicare beneficiaries who use insulin would have paid nothing out of pocket for the drug and their injection supplies during the emergency, removing a cost barrier at a time when people were being told to stay home and avoid in-person visits. Beneficiaries who preferred to avoid trips to the pharmacy could have had insulin and supplies shipped to their homes.

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates all deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance for insulin and associated medical supplies under Medicare Part D and Medicare Advantage during the COVID-19 emergency period.
Applies the same cost-sharing elimination to low-income subsidy-eligible Part D beneficiaries, harmonizing their coverage with the emergency rule.

Requires prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage prescription drug plans to let beneficiaries fill or refill insulin and supplies by mail order to their home, at the beneficiary's option, during the emergency.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government and Medicare Part D plans would absorb the cost of the eliminated copays and deductibles; premiums or plan payments would adjust accordingly. The bill does not touch insulin manufacturers' list prices, so taxpayers would be paying more for a drug whose underlying price stays the same.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and Medicare Part D plans

drawbacks.text: The relief is temporary, lasting only for the COVID-19 emergency period, and the bill provides no payment mechanism beyond existing plan financing, so the added cost would fall on the Medicare program and Part D plans rather than addressing drug prices directly.
The bill leaves insulin manufacturers' list prices untouched, so it pays for more access without lowering what the country ultimately pays for the underlying drug.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries who need insulin, the benefit is direct and immediate: no out-of-pocket cost for a medically necessary drug during a national emergency, plus the option of home delivery. The costs are real but diffuse — higher federal and plan spending — and the temporary scope means the underlying problem of insulin prices is left for another day. It is a narrow, emergency-period fix rather than a lasting solution.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees, and neither committee took it up before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021, so it died without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 28, 2020, with 25 other original cosponsors joining sponsor Rep. Maxine Waters.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Ways and Means Committee.
No further action was recorded: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries who use insulin kept paying their usual copays during the emergency. Part D plans and insulin manufacturers were spared any change in how insulin is paid for; the cost barrier and the existing pricing arrangement stayed in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and drug makers kept the status quo

for.name: Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to eliminate Medicare cost-sharing for insulin during the COVID-19 emergency.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill.

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral for relevant provisions and never took the bill up.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 43 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsors are recorded, and the House never took a vote that would show a fuller split.

industries.note: Zero cost-sharing would remove a barrier to filling prescriptions, likely increasing insulin volume during the emergency, and the bill leaves list prices untouched, so manufacturers keep their pricing. Patients and manufacturers both gain, though taxpayers absorb the added cost.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Plans would have to cover insulin and supplies with no deductible, copay, or coinsurance, absorbing costs under existing plan financing. The industry has no independent say in the record here; its interest ran against the bill's beneficiary protections.
Plans must let beneficiaries choose mail-order delivery of insulin and supplies, expanding the mail-order channel during the emergency.
